description_full: Oil-Dri Corporation of America, together with its subsidiaries, develops, manufactures, and markets sorbent products in the United States and internationally. It operates in two segments: Retail and Wholesale Products Group, and Business to Business Products Group. The company provides agricultural and horticultural products, including mineral-based absorbent products that serve as carriers for biological and chemical active ingredients, drying agents, and growing media under the Agsorb, Verge, and Flo-Fre brand names. It also offers animal health and nutrition products for the livestock industry; and adsorbent products for bleaching, purification, and filtration applications. In addition, it provides cat litter products under the Cat's Pride and Jonny Cat brands, including scoopable litters, non-clumping litters, probiotic crystal litters, cat litter accessories, and antibacterial clumping litter products; crystal cat litter products under the Ultra Pet brand; animal health and nutrition products under the Amlan brand; industrial and automotive sorbent products under the Oil-Dri brand; sports field products under the Pro's Choice brand; fluids purification products under the Pure-Flo brand; renewable diesel pretreatment adsorbents under the Metal-X and Metal-Z brands; agricultural products under the Agsorb brand; and lawn and garden products under the Verge brand. Its customers include mass merchandisers, farm and fleet channel, drugstore chains, pet specialty retail outlets, dollar stores, retail grocery stores, distributors of industrial cleanup and automotive products, environmental service companies, and sports field product and sports turf material users; processors and refiners of edible oils, petroleum-based oils, and biodiesel fuel; manufacturers of animal feed and agricultural chemicals; distributors of animal health and nutrition products; and marketers of consumer products. The company was founded in 1941 and is based in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Oil-Dri Corporation Of America is a small-cap basic materials business with a $1.0B market cap on $494M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +7% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 25% against a 8% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $46M in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.41× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 31× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 2.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.8% of the shares.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 58% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 29% over the last three months.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 9.9% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 25% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.49).
It runs a 27% gross margin and converts 9% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.41x.
ROE of 19% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).

hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $73.7M (7% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.1% over 3 years, 10.1% over 5 years and 6.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.

Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.5x, 6.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 18, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.8%, and institutions hold 75%.
It returns 2.2% a year to shareholders (1.2% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 7.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 927 employees, each generates about $533K of revenue, 0.8x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 5.3% a year.
That works out to $50K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (5x revenue per employee).
